newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Delta says no early capital needs.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Delta says no early capital needs.

text.p: Delta Gold NL said on Thursday it did not anticipate any need to raise capital from the market until at least early 1998.
Chairman Peter Vanderspuy said after the annual meeting the company could fund all existing proposals from cash and debt.

These included repaying joint venture partner Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd for its 33 percent share in the Hartley platinum project in Zimbabwe, the Eureka gold project in Zimbabwe, and the Kanowna Mining Centre and Mulgarrie gold project, renamed Golden Feather, in Western Australia.
"There's not a need for us to come back to shareholders with what's on our book at the moment," Vanderspuy told reporters.
He earlier blamed "an incorrect perception in the market place that Delta is about to make a major call on capital" as one of the reasons for the decline in Delta's share price.
The share price during the past three months has eased from about A$3.40 to Thursday's close of A$2.40.

Vanderspuy also blamed a lacklustre gold price and strong Australian dollar, negative investor sentiment towards Africa, and perceptions that BHP was not committed to the Hartley project for the fall.
He said he expected that both Golden Feather and Eureka were likely to reach go-ahead decisions during 1997 and achieve first production by mid-1998.
Eureka would require capital costs of A$15-20 million and Golden Feather A$25 million.
The two projects "together exhibit the potential to produce around 150,000 ounces per year", he said.
Delta did not need to repay BHP for its share of the capital costs of the US$264 million Hartley project, but would increase it share of revenue by doing so, he said.
This decision would not have to be made until after 1996/97 following delays that have pushed back the build-up to full production at Hartley until the final quarter of calender 1997.

Vanderspuy said BHP and Delta should also have concluded an analysis by the end of 1997 on whether to double production at Hartley from its initial 2.16 million tonnes a year at a cost of US$150 million.

He also noted that the current low share price could leave the company open to an opportunistic bid, but told reporters a bid would not succeed as Delta was protected by its large institutional shareholders, who were seeking long-term growth.
